data.title: Fintech firms rethink cybersecurity as AI advances
data.description:
Executives warn that AI advances could expose payment systems to cyberattacks and erode customer trust.

Financial technology (fintech) executives are raising concerns about cybersecurity as advances in artificial intelligence (AI) increase the risks of attacks on financial systems, with companies facing growing demands to protect their infrastructure and maintain customer trust.

Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 20 November, Tazapay Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Rahul Shinghal said cybersecurity had become a major concern for fintech companies, which already face challenges involving regulatory approvals, scaling operations and cross-border payments.

"Cybersecurity is just top of mind for all of us right now," he said.

He said the company has redirected almost 80% of its engineering capacity towards building cybersecurity defences over the past two quarters. "It is just the reality now."

NIUM Founder and Chief Executive Officer Prajit Nanu also highlighted the risks posed by more advanced AI models, saying the potential for cyberattacks had become a major concern after 11 years of building the payments company.

"Now, with the new AI models, our ability to get hacked is so crazy. It is scary right now," he said during the panel discussion.

Nanu said fintech companies were investing time in strengthening their systems as AI models became increasingly capable.

Addo AI Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Ayesha Khanna said cybersecurity was also a major concern amongst the banks she advises. She pointed to the challenges of securing legacy infrastructure, saying banks could not patch their systems quickly enough.

"There's just so much legacy infrastructure, which is an advantage to the fintechs at the moment, but the speed at which they can patch their systems is limited, and they just can't move fast enough," said Khanna.

She warned that security failures could undermine customer confidence. "And I think that this one mistake can ruin the trust that customers have."

Khanna also cited a cyber incident involving Optimizely, a platform used for A/B testing. She said the incident affected 186 companies and that attackers had sought to access cryptocurrency wallets.

She said the potential loss of customer confidence was a longer-term concern, comparing the consequences to a bank run.

The panel also considered how fintech companies should balance investment in existing businesses with expansion into new areas.

Pine Labs Chief Executive Officer Amrish Rau said that companies should focus on building a strong business in one market rather than spreading themselves too thinly. A profitable core business can provide the resources to fund other opportunities, he said.

Rau also said fintech companies had yet to realise the full potential of their existing markets, with the sector capable of compounding at 25% to 30% over 20 years.

Companies should build on their existing strengths and extend them into newer areas, rather than pursue expansion without a clear strategy.

He cautioned against both refusing to change direction and pivoting too frequently. Companies need to decide whether to invest in new infrastructure or broaden their capabilities into areas such as technology and AI.

Nanu said fintech companies needed to dominate the segments where they had a competitive advantage rather than spread themselves too thinly across markets.

He said NIUM had identified three segments where it believed it could compete effectively and establish itself as a leader, whilst acknowledging that it was less competitive in other markets, such as Africa.

The panel also turned to the security requirements of agentic payments, as AI agents take on a greater role in initiating and executing financial transactions.

When asked which factors would provide a competitive advantage in an agent-driven business environment, Khanna identified trust and execution.

Nanu, however, said deep integration would be important because AI agents would prioritise the fastest and cheapest way to complete transactions.

Shinghal agreed, saying fintech companies needed to understand the parties and underlying activities behind transactions to determine whether they were legitimate.

He said companies needed to go beyond conventional know-your-customer and know-your-business checks to understand individual transactions and the agents involved.

Shinghal said this required gathering information from public and private databases and using transaction-monitoring models to identify suspicious behaviour. He also highlighted the need for compliance, liability, and governance frameworks as agentic payments develop.

He said that the technology enabling communication between AI agents was only a small part of what was needed to make these transactions work securely.

data.title: How Monzo made mission and profitability inseparable
data.description:
Transparent treatment builds trust that drives product use and referrals, says Monzo vice chair.

Two thirds of Monzo’s new customers in the UK come through word of mouth, and TS Anil, who led the bank for six years as CEO, says that is what happens when a mission statement becomes an actual business model.

Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival, Anil, vice chairman of Monzo’s group board, said the defining choice he made when he took over as CEO was to treat the company’s mission and business plan as inseparable rather than as a trade-off.

“A mission without a business plan is a freaking bumper sticker,” he said. “How do you create a mission that’s congruent with a business plan?”

Monzo’s mission is to make money work for everyone. Anil said too many companies operate with a dichotomy: they claim one mission whilst making money in a way that contradicts it. The result, he said, is that it starts to feel like a trade-off.

His argument is that the two can and should reinforce each other. If the mission is executed correctly, customers are genuinely helped, treated transparently, and not exploited. The result is trust, and trust produces what Anil calls customer love.

“The average Monzo review is seven times or more likely to use words like love when describing us,” he said.

Customer love drives deeper product engagement, greater willingness to buy additional products, and referrals to friends and family. Those referrals produce growth. Monzo adds a million customers a quarter in the UK alone, and two thirds of those arrive through word of mouth.

“The more successful you are from a business plan perspective, the more customers you’re able to serve, the more you fuel the mission,” Anil said. “So these two things are not divergent at all.”

He was equally direct about what the approach is not. It is not about offering freebies to customers at the expense of investors and calling that mission. Monzo’s principle is to never monetise what he called the troika of incumbent revenue: customer ignorance, inertia, or vulnerability. Removing those options forces a different kind of product thinking, one that finds its commercial model in genuinely serving customers rather than in exploiting their behaviour.

At Monzo, Anil said, the mission is not a poster on the wall or something that features on a mouse pad. It is the standard against which every decision is tested. “The number of all hands where someone would stand up and ask me, TS, why are we doing that thing? That doesn’t feel like it’s on mission. We should address that,” he said.

The growth model, he said, becomes self-reinforcing as the mission is served more effectively. “When you have people tell you that their kids trust their kids’ money with you, and the fact that that’s what drives our growth — it happens because, as I said, the mission makes it all happen,” he said.

data.title: Domestic wholesale sales rise 19.5% to $139.4b in Q3
data.description:
Chemicals and chemical products sales surged 90.3% YoY during the period.

Singapore’s domestic wholesale sales increased 19.5% year-on-year to $139.4b in the third quarter, according to data from the Department of Statistics.

Excluding petroleum, domestic wholesale sales rose 21.3% to $58.1b over the same period.

Most wholesale trade industries recorded higher domestic sales, led by chemicals and chemical products, which surged 90.3% YoY due to higher petrochemical prices.

Sales in the ship chandlers and bunkering industry also climbed 45.7%, driven by higher bunker fuel prices.

Meanwhile, sales of metals, timber and construction materials declined 29.6% due to lower metals sales.

On a seasonally adjusted quarter-on-quarter basis, domestic wholesale sales rose 8%, whilst sales excluding petroleum grew 2.2%.

data.title: Ant International links tokenised deposits and funds via new protocol
data.description:
The platform supports delivery-versus-payment transactions.

Ant International has launched the Whale Orchestration Protocol, enabling transactions between tokenised bank deposits and money market funds through its blockchain-based wholesale settlement platform, WhaleRTP.

The protocol supports delivery-versus-payment transactions between the two types of tokenised assets.

It was developed under the Monetary Authority of Singapore's Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency (BLOOM) initiative.

The group said it has completed pilot transactions with DBS and Franklin Templeton, which integrated their respective Treasury Tokens and Tokenised Money Market Fund solutions into WhaleRTP.

“As a full-stack financial solutions provider, 24/7 real-time liquidity management is essential for our business,” Kelvin Li, General Manager of Platform Tech and Senior Vice President at Ant International, said.

“We look forward to scaling this solution with more partners so businesses worldwide can access next-generation treasury management solutions,” Li added.

data.title: MAS to expand tokenised bill use for collateral management in 2027
data.description:
The plan follows the $100m issuance of four-week tokenised bills.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) plans to expand the use of tokenised MAS Bills for collateral management in 2027, following a $100m issuance that attracted applications worth more than twice the amount offered.

MAS also plans to increase tokenised bill issuances and bring in more participating financial institutions.

The central bank said the issuance could pave the way for secured lending transactions involving tokenised assets on the Singapore Dollar Test Network.

It also aims to test wider use of tokenised securities in financial market activities to potentially improve settlement efficiency.

The expansion plans follow the issuance of four-week tokenised bills on 6 November through the MAS-operated Singapore Dollar Test Network. 

The bills were settled using wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC).

MAS said five primary dealers participated in the auction, which received applications amounting to more than double the issuance size. The bills will mature on 4 December.

The bills were issued directly on the digital network rather than being issued conventionally and subsequently tokenised, eliminating the need for certain reconciliation processes and intermediaries.

The issuance follows a live interbank overnight lending transaction settled using wholesale CBDC in 2025.

data.title: NETS and ANT to explore AI-initiated payments
data.description:
NETS App wallet users would grant authorisation to the agents.

Network for Electronic Transfers (NETS) and Ant International have inked a pact to bring artificial intelligence (AI)-powered payments to everyday transactions in Singapore as agentic commerce gains traction.

Under a memorandum of understanding (MOU), NETS will become the first national payment network to join Ant International's Agentic Mobile Protocol (AMP), an agentic payment protocol designed for mobile interfaces.

The partnership will explore how NETS App wallet users can grant trusted authorisation for AI agents to initiate and complete payments through AMP.

It will also explore the deployment of AMP across NETS' merchant acquiring infrastructure.

This would enable NETS merchants, ranging from heartland stalls to large enterprises, to accept AI-initiated payments.

The two parties will also explore interoperability between Know-Your-Agent frameworks to enable more efficient onboarding and strengthen trust, accountability, and risk visibility across both ecosystems.

The MOU was signed at the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026.

data.title: PM Wong pushes wider APAC free trade amidst global divisions
data.description:
He called for WTO reforms to strengthen the rules-based global trading system. 

Asia-Pacific economies must advance plans for a regional free trade area by building on existing agreements amidst growing geopolitical tensions, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

Wong, at the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, called for concrete steps towards a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, building on the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership and Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership.

“Our approach should be open and inclusive, to reinforce rather than to divide the wider trading system,” he said.

He also called for reforms to strengthen the World Trade Organization (WTO) and uphold a rules-based multilateral trading system.

Meanwhile, Wong warned that geopolitical tensions and growing national security concerns were contributing to a more fragmented global economy.

“We should not allow our region to become divided into competing economic blocs,” he said. “We must keep the Asia-Pacific open and connected.”

Wong also urged APEC economies to pursue more flexible trade arrangements when reaching agreement amongst all members proves difficult.

He cited the WTO's E-Commerce Agreement and Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement as examples of initiatives that allow participating economies to cooperate without requiring universal agreement.

New initiatives such as the Green Economy Partnership and Future of Investment and Trade Partnership could also provide opportunities for cooperation.

“We should pursue a more flexible and pragmatic approach towards multilateralism – to allow willing partners to move ahead, demonstrate what works, and keep the door open for others to join when they are ready,” Wong said.

He added that regional economic cooperation should produce practical benefits for businesses, including making cross-border trade easier.

data.title: Treat AI agents as shoppers, not bankers: Google's Jeremy Goro
data.description:
AI agents must not invent a shadow financial system.

Deploying AI agents in the financial industry must involve strict boundaries where they are just shoppers and not bankers.

“AI agents must speak the language of these [payment] rails, not invent a shadow financial system,” Jeremy Goro, head of financial services strategy & partnerships, EMEA at Google, told attendees of the Policy Stage of Singapore Fintech Festival 2026 on 19 November.

AI agents must be trusted expert shoppers, not shadow bankers, Goro said in a panel moderated by Jo Yeon, a director at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

Goro emphasized the need to establish clear technical boundaries for AI, and for payment execution and Know-Your-Customer to remain with licensed banks, established payment networks, and payment service providers, Goro said.

“We need to preserve the established liability and consumer protections because innovation cannot come at the expense of consumer rights,” Goro said.

Goro said that the industry must work to have tamper-proof cryptographic electronic sign mandates for autonomous commerce. This meant having strict limits like a maximum price, merchant criteria, and expiration timeline for AI agents executing a transaction.

“The real opportunity lies in anchoring autonomous AI directly into trusted national rails and consumer protections that have already been protecting billions of users every day,” Goro said.

Goro was joined at the panel by Kelvin Li, senior vice president at Ant International, and Jesse McWaters, EVP, head of global policy at Mastercard.

Li expects agentic AI payments to make up 50% of all payment activity by 2030 and it will be normalized enough that “payments will just happen,” Li said.

“Previously, we were looking at payments from a transaction perspective. So now we will be looking at a task perspective,” Li said.

Li said that the future payment system will need to be able to handle cross-border nanopayments.

McWaters, meanwhile, warned that inadequate liability and fraud protections may discourage banks and merchants from accepting AI agent transactions. But he also asked regulators to approach agentic commerce not just with risk in mind but also to consider the opportunities.

“In many cases, I think what's really required in order to deliver on that is thinking about how those regulations and that guidance should be evolved to meet the needs of an evolving ecosystem, rather than trying to  slap some new regulations on top of the existing frameworks,” McWaters said.

data.title: Payment networks face governance hurdles in cross-border expansion
data.description:
Executives flag pricing, dispute and fraud concerns across different jurisdictions. 

Differences in payment rules, commercial incentives, and dispute procedures are complicating efforts to connect national payment networks across borders, executives said at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 19 November.

Joyce Bo, executive vice president for core payments in Asia Pacific at Mastercard, said national QR payment schemes typically use push payments, whilst card networks and many mobile wallets rely on pull payments.

These systems have different messaging, authentication and settlement models, requiring technical integration alongside common commercial and regulatory arrangements, she said in a panel discussion.

Moreover, payment operators must reconcile differences in pricing, merchant arrangements and dispute rules to make cross-border connections commercially sustainable.

"Every participant needs to have the right incentives, and consumers need to continue to be protected," she added.

Andrew McCormack, CEO of Nexus Global Payments, said connecting payment systems also requires a common framework establishing the roles and responsibilities of participating institutions.

"Nexus is a technology platform, but probably more importantly, it's a scheme rule book," he said.

McCormack said the framework covers dispute resolution and how the network interacts with domestic systems such as India's Unified Payments Interface and Singapore's PayNow and FAST.

He added that banks and payment service providers remain responsible for authenticating their customers, whilst disputes involving fraud, human error or technical failures require established procedures.

Carlos Álvarez, chief risk officer at FLAR, said cross-border connections introduce additional participants, including foreign exchange and settlement providers, which can create operational risks.

"For instance, in smaller markets, will these providers be reliable and able to provide the services 24/7 and the like?" Álvarez said.

He also raised concerns about differences in how jurisdictions prevent fraud and recover funds. "Because in practice, what happens when there is a risk is that you have different standards for dealing with fraud, right? So the level of maturity between countries is different.”

Meanwhile, Mike Truter, head of industry engagement at Swift, identified regulatory reporting obligations, capital and foreign exchange controls, and inconsistent market practices as major obstacles in the final stage of cross-border payments.

He said addressing these issues requires coordinated action amongst policymakers, payment infrastructure operators, financial institutions and technology providers.

"It's not as simple as one pays; everyone has to pay. Everyone plays the game," Truter said.

Sohini Rajola, executive director for growth at the National Payments Corporation of India, said the commercial design of cross-border connections should prioritise reducing costs for consumers and merchants before determining how expenses are shared.

She said intermediaries must find ways to make transactions faster and cheaper without passing additional costs to end users.

"If there are incentives which don't align for that, you can have anything on paper as a blueprint. It's not going to be able to succeed or scale," Rajola said.

Despite these challenges, payment networks are pursuing additional international connections.

McCormack said Nexus plans to begin a pilot involving Singapore and Malaysia in 2027, followed by India and other participating markets.

Álvarez also highlighted Project Lumina, which is working with five Latin American central banks to assess the technical, regulatory and commercial requirements for future cross-border payment integration.
